summary: Level-order traversal where the direction alternates each level (left-to-right, then right-to-left).
mainInsight: Do a normal BFS and reverse every other level's values. Your deque variant instead pops from alternating ends and prepends children in mirrored order so the deque is always in the right order for the next level.

approaches.name: BFS + reverse alternate levels
approaches.summary: Collect each level normally; reverse it when the direction flag is right-to-left.

approaches.name: BFS with a deque popping from alternating ends
approaches.summary: Pop from the left and append children to the right on L-to-R levels; pop from the right and appendleft on R-to-L levels.

approaches.name: DFS with a deque per level
approaches.summary: Append left or appendleft depending on level parity.

personalSolution.approach: BFS with a deque popping from alternating ends
personalSolution.notes: Correct and O(n). The reverse-alternate-levels version is easier to explain.

promptVariants: What is the simplest way to implement zigzag order?
options: Level-order BFS with alternate levels reversed
Two stacks only with no level tracking
cards.answer: Level-order BFS with alternate levels reversed
cards.explanation: The set of nodes per level is the same as normal level order; only the order within alternate levels changes.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Two stacks only with no level tracking: Two stacks do work but must be paired with level separation.

promptVariants: Why does popping from the right and prepending children (right then left) keep the next level correctly ordered?
cards.answer: On a right-to-left level the nodes are consumed from the right end; their children are put on the left end with appendleft(right child) then appendleft(left child), so after the level the deque holds the next level in left-to-right order again (the next pop-from-left level). The mirrored handling on the other parity keeps the invariant that the deque is always in the order the next level will be consumed.
cards.explanation: A flag-and-reverse solution is easier to defend.

promptVariants: What is the queue space and what does Python's deque give you?
Why is a deque (not a list) used?
cards.answer: O(w) for the widest level. A deque offers O(1) appends/pops at both ends; with a plain list popleft/insert(0) would be O(n).

promptVariants: What is the zigzag traversal of [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]?
cards.explanation: Level 1 (0-based) is right-to-left: 20, 9; levels 0 and 2 are left-to-right.
